summary: A glossary of terms used in the IETF when discussing internationalization, meant to frame discussions in various areas and introduce the main ideas to participants. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 6365.

eli5.summary: Different languages use different letters and symbols. This is a dictionary of the words people use when they talk about making the internet work for all of them.

subtitle: A glossary of terms for discussing internationalization in IETF standards work

tldr.problem: IETF working groups frequently need to discuss internationalization but lack consistent vocabulary, leading to confusion around terms like language versus script, character encoding forms versus schemes, and normalization.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3536 defines over 50 key terms used in internationalization discussions, covering fundamental concepts (language, script, character), standards bodies (ISO, Unicode Consortium), and character handling techniques (normalization, case, collation).
tldr.outcome: The glossary provides IETF participants with shared terminology to frame discussions on adding non-ASCII text support to protocols. It was replaced by RFC 6365.

today: RFC 3536 is Informational and was replaced by RFC 6365, which provides updated internationalization terminology. However, the core concepts and terms defined here remain valid for understanding how IETF protocols handle international text.

sections.title: Internationalization Terminology
sections.content:
Internationalization is making Internet protocols handle text from any language and script. As RFC 2277 notes, "internationalization is for humans"—protocols themselves do not need internationalization, but the text strings they carry do.

RFC 3536 provides a glossary of terms used in IETF discussions of internationalization. The document's purpose is to help frame discussions across IETF working groups and introduce main concepts to participants who may lack internationalization expertise. The definitions draw from ISO/IEC 10646, the Unicode Standard, the W3C Character Model, and earlier IETF documents. For many terms, the RFC notes the source in angle brackets, and provides commentary, examples, and context beyond the definitions themselves.
sections.eli5: Different parts of the internet need to talk about using different languages and alphabets. This document explains the words people use in those conversations.

sections.title: Fundamental Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines core terms needed for understanding internationalization. Language is how humans interact through speech, writing, or signing. A script is the set of graphic characters used for written language. Although the terms are often confused, they are distinct: a single script (like Latin) can be used for many languages, and a single language (like Mongolian) can be written with multiple scripts.

Character is a member of a set used for organization or representation of data, identified by its name rather than its shape. Coded character pairs a character with its numeric representation. A coded character set (CCS) defines the relationship between characters and their codes.

A character encoding form maps a character set to code units, while a character encoding scheme (CES) adds byte serialization. Charset is the combination of one or more CCSs with a CES. The RFC notes that charset is preferred over the ambiguous term "character set" in protocol specifications. Internationalization (i18n) means adding or improving non-ASCII text handling in a protocol. Localization (l10n) is adapting an internationalized application to a specific culture or language.
sections.eli5: Language is the words people speak. Script is how you write them down. A character is a single letter or symbol. All these pieces come together to let the internet work in any language.

sections.title: Standards Bodies and Character Standards
sections.content:
ISO/IEC 10646 is the primary international standard for character encoding, overseen by the group ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 2 WG2. It describes a coded character set covering nearly all known written characters. The Unicode Consortium produces the Unicode Standard, whose repertoire and code points are identical to ISO/IEC 10646 but with additional character properties like case conversion and numeric values.

For representing ISO/IEC 10646 characters on the wire, several transformation formats exist. UCS-2 and UCS-4 are the basic encoding forms. UTF-8 (defined in RFC 2279) is the preferred encoding for IETF protocols, using one to four octets per character while maintaining compatibility with US-ASCII. UTF-16, UTF-16BE, and UTF-16LE use two or four octets per character with byte-order variations. Before ISO/IEC 10646, many countries developed their own character sets; examples include ISO 8859-5 for Cyrillic and Shift-JIS for Japanese. These native charsets are still in use on the Internet today.
sections.eli5: Different groups have made standards for how to represent characters. The biggest ones are ISO and Unicode, which include almost every letter from every language. UTF-8 is the version most internet protocols use.

sections.title: Character Handling and Text Rendering
sections.content:
Several concepts are essential to handling text correctly across scripts and languages. A combining character modifies the display of the preceding non-combining character. A composite sequence is a non-combining character followed by one or more combining characters; the display engine must either find a glyph combining all of them or render the combination.

Normalization transforms text to a standard form so that visually identical strings can be compared for equivalence. For example, the letter "a with acute" might be stored as a single precomposed character or as the letter "a" followed by a combining acute accent. Normalization selects one representation as the canonical form. Case is the distinction between uppercase and lowercase letters; case mapping is the association between them. Collation is the ordering of text units, typically language-specific. Sorting physically arranges records according to a collation order.

Text can be displayed on a visual device or rendered for audio or tactile output. Glyph is an abstract form or image selected to represent a character during composition. Glyph code is a numeric reference to a glyph within a specific font. Transcoding converts text from one character encoding form to another without parsing the content.
sections.eli5: Some letters have marks on top (like 'é'). Combining characters make those marks, but sometimes they're stored separately from the base letter. Sorting is about putting text in order, which is different in different languages.

sections.title: Text in IETF Protocols
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols handle text that is entered by or visible to humans, requiring careful attention to internationalization. The RFC defines repertoire as the collection of characters in a character set. It notes that display and rendering of text may be complicated by combining marks that interact with each other, or by complex display rules for scripts like Arabic and Indic.

Internationalization affects multiple aspects of protocol design. Protocols must decide which character sets to support, whether to require normalization before comparison, how to handle case sensitivity in different scripts, and whether to support script-specific features like right-to-left rendering. The RFC emphasizes that many protocols historically handled only ASCII or a single script, leaving international support to local guesswork, which leads to interoperability problems. Adding proper internationalization support allows protocols to work across all scripts and languages.
sections.eli5: Internet protocols that let people type or read text need to handle languages from everywhere. If they only work with English letters, people in other countries can't use them properly.
